scope: Implementing A/B tests in client apps and web: assignment (deterministic hashing, stickiness), exposure logging at the point of use, control as the safe default, local override for testing, the experiment-design minimums an implementer must honour (pre-registered metric, sample size, no peeking, SRM check), the evaluation-API shape across vendors, and platform-owner rules (Apple, Google Play/Firebase, Microsoft Azure, Google Search). Out of scope: statistical analysis engines and multi-armed bandits beyond what an implementer must honour.
research_type: Technology / software, with Statistical / data claims (MED-HIGH bar)

questions.text: Best practices: what is current best practice for this topic?
Known solutions: what solutions, patterns, libraries and tools already exist, and how do they compare?
Platform guidelines: what do the platform owners' own guidelines say, for each platform the topic touches (Apple, Android, Windows, web, the databases and runtimes concerned)?
The expert's view: if we hired an expert consultant in this topic, what would they tell us: what to do, what to avoid, and what people usually get wrong?

methodology.method: guidelines/researching/process/research-methodology-and-sources: orient, go to authoritative sources (specifications, platform-owner and vendor docs first; peer-reviewed practitioner papers for the statistical claims), chain citations from the exp-platform.com index, corroborate across independent sources, record provenance at generation time.
methodology.search_strategy: WebSearch for each vendor and platform's own documentation and for the canonical experimentation literature (Kohavi et al. 2009 survey; Dmitriev et al. KDD 2017; Fabijan et al. KDD 2019; Microsoft ExP articles); every cited page fetched with WebFetch or curl (OpenFeature spec fetched raw from its repository; PDFs read directly).
methodology.inclusion: Primary sources: open specifications (OpenFeature), platform-owner documentation and policy (Apple, Google, Microsoft), vendor documentation for their own SDKs, peer-reviewed practitioner papers. Secondary sources only where no primary covered the point (Statsig engineering blog; Evan Miller's article), flagged in trust basis.
methodology.exclusion: Search-result snippets, third-party SEO/CRO blogs, pages that could not be fetched (Statsig FAQ 404, Optimizely forced-decision pages redirected), and any claim not backed by a fetched quote.
methodology.scoring: guidelines/researching/evidence/verification-and-trust-scoring: Authority 30 + Independent corroboration 25 + Accuracy 20 + Currency 10 + Transparency 15, capped by the domain bar (Technical MEDIUM; Statistical MED-HIGH for experiment-design claims).

summary: Both existing rules hold. A variant-by-key evaluation interface is the common shape (OpenFeature, LaunchDarkly, GrowthBook, Azure), but every standard and SDK makes the caller pass a default value and never throws; control is the abort/kill-switch state; forced variants for QA are a standard property of experimentation systems and dev tooling should be off in production. The topic is missing the implementer's core duties: deterministic hash of user+experiment ID with stable assignment through ramp-ups, exposure logged where the variant is actually seen, pre-registered metric and minimum sample size, no peeking, an SRM check on every experiment, A/A tests, ramp-up with auto-abort, data-quality guards (client telemetry loss, bots, Twyman's law), novelty effects, web flicker, Google Search rules (no cloaking, 302, canonical, end tests), Apple's rules (variants in the reviewed binary, described in review notes, no downloaded code) and store-page tests through Apple product page optimization and Google Play store listing experiments.
open_questions: Whether the interface should return a variant name (String) or a typed value: OpenFeature returns typed values and exposes the variant name only in evaluation details; the owner decides which the rule names.
Whether Apple App Review treats server-switched UI variants already in the binary as 'hidden features' under 2.5.19: no Apple text addresses A/B tests inside apps directly.
Cross-device stickiness: the sources establish stickiness only for the same user identifier; no primary source establishes a general mechanism across anonymous devices.
limitations: Windows desktop (Microsoft Store) has no fetched first-party A/B guidance; Microsoft coverage is Azure App Configuration and Microsoft ExP research.

Several vendor quotes (Optimizely bucketing, Firebase, Play, Statsig, LaunchDarkly) came through a fetch summariser that returns quoted sentences rather than whole pages; trust scores account for this.
Statsig's FAQ on one-sided manual exposure imbalance returned 404 and is not cited; Optimizely forced-decision pages redirected and are not cited.
Kohavi et al.'s book 'Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments' (2020) was not accessible; its authors' peer-reviewed papers stand in for it.
Evan Miller's article and the Statsig blog are secondary sources, used only where corroborated.
license: MIT (this research record); quoted material remains under its sources' terms and is quoted for verification.
